what: 50 cm key-band comparison, three arms sharing one frozen broadband stimulus, judged with a model fitted from 50 cm data (not the 115 cm model)

conditions.source: full-band white noise, RMS-normalised, identical samples for all arms
conditions.arms: open = feedback path disconnected but the source still plays; bypass = loop closed without canceller; cancel = loop closed with the candidate

the_decisive_comparison: The same 400 Hz band, same 50 cm geometry: with the 115 cm model the canceller made it +3.22 dB WORSE; with the 50 cm model it is 3.62 dB better. A 6.8 dB swing from fitting at the right geometry.
reading: In every band where the loop actually adds level (200, 250, 400, 800, 3150 Hz) the fitted canceller reduces the closed-loop level, by 1.2 to 4.3 dB.
In the three bands where the loop does not boost (125, 500, 630 Hz) it makes things up to 2.2 dB worse; that is reported, not hidden.

This is the first result that shows a 50 cm working point with a measurable, explainable benefit, and it explains why the earlier 322 Hz test said nothing: that single frequency is not where the loop boosts at this distance.
limits: one run, one 16384-frame window per arm
the levelling stopped at -20.84 dBFS mic peak (adjustment cap), below the -12 dBFS target
nothing here is a claim about distances other than 50 cm
